M2.lead_interest: How people understand, and decide whether to trust and go along with, adaptive AI systems that act on their personal data, and how to measure that understanding beyond engagement metrics.
M2.notes: Claims about Riley stay within the ground-truth boundaries: note-taker role, analyst title, class projects and the AI Coach numbers are all accurate, and faculty content is left as placeholders with only a generic program sentence. The lead interest stays on understanding rather than privacy, but it leans more on 'trust and measurement' than on Riley's 'still have a say' agency framing, and it omits details from the voice sample such as users turning off health-data sharing.

REV.lead_interest: What people think is happening when an app uses their own data to make choices for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say.
REV.notes: Claims stay within the ground truth: research experience is tied to undergraduate coursework, note-taking stays note-taking, and 'roughly one in ten' is hedged as an impression, which matches Riley's own phrasing in the voice sample. The Why Khoury section is still an unfilled placeholder, so there are no faculty claims to evaluate.

faculty_misdescriptions.quote: and that privacy concerns and trust held up better as a result
faculty_misdescriptions.why: The snapshot supports only that risk-contingent autonomy improves perceived control. The added downstream result on privacy concerns and trust is not in the ground truth, so it is an invented finding.

M3.notes: The email keeps Riley's agency-and-understanding framing, states the analyst role and lack of publications honestly, and labels AI Coach as simpler than an LLM agent. The one problem is an embellished description of the COLM'26 finding that goes beyond the snapshot.

cross.revision_change_summary: REV replaces M2's metrics-forward, analyst-credential framing (owning the launch experiment, 20 A/B tests a year, power calculations, SQL/Python, and goals of changing how AI features are evaluated) with a plainer, personal framing centered on listening to users. It focuses on what people think is happening when an app uses their data and whether they feel they still have a say, and it explicitly disclaims interest in engagement or accuracy.
